title: Adaptive ancestor-graph caching for cross-request KV reuse
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Our current KV cache stores prefix key/value blobs keyed at the request-level which leads to duplication when many requests share overlapping prompt fragments (e.g., system + user templates + few-shot examples). This inflates GPU memory usage and reduces effective cache hit rates under high concurrency and continuous batching.

Proposal: Implement an ancestor-graph based canonicalization layer that decomposes incoming prompts into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of canonical prompt segments (nodes). Each node is content-addressed (stable hash after canonicalization) and maps to a reusable KV fragment (value = cached past KV slice). On request arrival we compute a compact fingerprint of the ancestor graph and query the fragment index to assemble a reuse plan: exact fragment reuse, partial reuse with stitched KV, or fall back to full decoding.

Key design points:
- Canonicalization: normalize whitespace, slot placeholders, and template parameter ordering to increase hit rate. Keep canon rules conservative to avoid semantic collisions.
- Chunking strategy: use token-aware boundary detection (prefer semantic boundaries, not fixed bytes) and a rolling Rabin-based fingerprint for shardable fragments.
- Fragment index: compact in-memory hash table on host CPU; index entries point to GPU slab references (shard_id, offset, length). Use 64-bit content hashes.
- Storage: GPU memory stores KV fragments in slab-allocated pools; fragments are reference-counted by active in-flight requests and background pinned metrics.
- Eviction: hierarchical eviction combining global LRU by fragment reuse score and slab-level compaction window. Periodic compaction coalesces adjacent fragments when safe.
- Consistency: allow eventual consistency between CPU index and GPU slab (background reconciliation) with guarded fallbacks to avoid incorrect KV use that could corrupt decoding.
- Latency/overhead: fingerprint + index lookup must be bounded (<250us p50 on host) to avoid negating batching gains. Provide opt-in aggressive heuristics (probabilistic LSH) behind feature flag.

Implementation plan (phased):
1) Prototype canonicalization + index in user-space runtime (CPU-only) and measure hit rate on sampled production traces. (Spike, 2w)
2) Integrate index lookup into continuous-batching admission path and build assembly path to convert fragment list -> request-specific KV mapping. Add safety checks to fall back if mismatch. (3w)
3) Implement GPU slab allocator and fragment store with reference-counting, evictions and compaction. Add metrics (reuse_rate, gpu_mem_saved, extra_lookup_latency, stitch_failures). (4w)
4) Canary rollout: runtime feature flag, 5% traffic, monitor p95 latency and failure modes, iterate. (2w)

Metrics & dashboards to add:
- Fragment reuse rate (per model, per route)
- Average GPU memory per active request
- Cache dedupe ratio (bytes deduped / total bytes)
- Extra host processing time per request p50/p95
- Stitch failure rate and fallbacks triggered

Risk analysis and trade-offs:
- False positives from aggressive canonicalization could change model outputs. Mitigation: conservative canonicalization + regression eval set to detect semantic deltas per rollout.
- Index lookup overhead can hurt low-latency p50; mitigation: microbenchmarks and optional sampling mode to build confidence before full enable.
- Increased complexity in GPU memory lifecycle; mitigation: strict feature flag, strong invariants and additional tracing to debug refcounts.

Rollout and release: feature behind runtime-1.20 gate with incremental canaries per region, route-level opt-in, and automatic rollback on quality regressions.
